1. What shipped (Tracks B/E/F/G, the audit, the 8-bug remediation)
2. The exact 8 bugs fixed, with commit SHAs
3. The root cause writeup — why this happened, pointing at the "found code needs same rigor" memory
4. What's still open — the 4 named test-coverage gaps as the concrete next step, the 41 unverified findings as backlog, and the explicit calibration note ("this does not mean entirety of happy path/corner cases is covered")
5. Where everything lives (memory index, specs, plans, the audit artifact URL)
6. A ready-to-paste starter prompt for the fresh session

Also updated .claude/plans/ACTIVE.md (was stale — still said Track B/E in progress) to reflect Track G shipping and the audit/remediation, with a pointer to the handoff doc.

Not yet committed to git — want me to commit the handoff doc + ACTIVE.md update now, or wait until just ci confirms green first?

Read .claude/plans/SESSION_HANDOFF.md and the memory index at
~/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/memory/MEMORY.md before doing anything else.

Confirm `just ci` is currently green on main — it was still running when the handoff was written,
so don't assume. If it's not green, fix whatever's red before anything else.

Then close the four test-coverage gaps in SESSION_HANDOFF.md §4 (npm::round_trip,
parse_publish_target/release_trigger, probe_git wiring, pre_cursor) one at a time via strict TDD —
red test first, confirmed failing, minimal fix or deletion, confirmed passing, independent
read-only review per fix (explicitly tell every reviewer agent it is read-only and must not run
git stash/checkout/reset/clean), commit. Don't batch them.

After that, tell me what you'd recommend for the remaining 41 unverified medium/low audit findings
(full list at the artifact URL in the handoff doc) rather than starting on them without asking —
that's a scope/priority call I want to make, not one to assume.

6	
7	---

32	
33	**8-bug remediation** — every CONFIRMED critical/high finding from the audit fixed via strict TDD
34	(red test reproducing the exact reported failure scenario → confirmed failing → minimal fix →
35	confirmed passing → independent read-only review → commit). One review-found gap (a fix that had
36	correct logic but an untested branch) was closed rather than accepted. See §2 for the list.

38	## 2. The 8 bugs fixed this session (all committed, all reviewed, all on `main`)
39	
40	1. `bca04b1` — `cargo_publish`'s pre-publish version guard couldn't parse `version.workspace = true`
41	   (the pattern all 10 of this repo's own crates use). Would have hard-failed `callisto publish` on
42	   this repo today. **This bug had ZERO test coverage when it shipped — see §3.**
43	2. `a700bba` — `PublishTarget::NuGet`/`GitHubRelease` silently no-opped the real publish while the
44	   release-tag gate still fired, claiming success with nothing published. Now an exhaustive match +
45	   ecosystem-mismatch validation at walk time (E119).
46	3. `2bb6ca4` + `c09c5f7` — arbitrary file write via unvalidated `changelog` path in `callisto.toml`,
47	   plus `changesets.dir`'s traversal guard missing the absolute-path case. Both now route through
48	   `callisto_model::path::workspace_relative`.
49	4. `bb194cc` — npm's manifest-controlled `publishConfig.registry` field was unvalidated and could
50	   redirect `npm publish`/`npm view` to an attacker host with `NPM_TOKEN` live in the environment.
51	   Now validated against the operator's `[registries]` allowlist (E120).
52	5. `6e16212` + `6b09e48` — subprocess timeout only killed the direct child, not descendants holding
53	   stdout/stderr pipes open, so `PUBLISH_TIMEOUT_SECS` could be defeated forever. Fixed with a
54	   bounded reader-thread grace period (channel-based, no `unsafe`, no process-group/libc calls —
55	   `unsafe_code = "forbid"` is a hard workspace invariant). Both the timeout-kill branch and the
56	   normal-exit branch are now independently tested.
57	6. `d353e54` — Cargo `round_trip` over-corrected a prior bound-crossing fix, bailing on ALL compound
58	   ranges with an upper bound instead of just ones the target actually crosses. The regression test
59	   that shipped alongside the original bug was named `..._is_rewritten` but asserted `is_none()` —
60	   the test documented the bug instead of catching it.
61	7. `def6862` — `[[package-set]]` ecosystem-prefixed glob patterns (`"cargo:pkg-*"`) matched zero
62	   packages, silently, because matching only ever checked the bare name. Independently rediscovered
63	   by 3 of the 8 audit dimension-finders from different angles. `GraphError::PackageSetMatchedNothing`
64	   existed as a safety net but was never constructed anywhere — now a real `DiagnosticCode` fires.
65	
66	Final `just ci` after all 8 fixes: **confirmed green** (all 7 phases — fmt-check, lint, test, audit,
67	doc-check, wasm-check, coverage — exit 0, verified clean, not just exit-code-trusted) on `def6862`,
68	run 2026-08-12. If you're picking this up later and other commits have landed since `def6862`,
69	re-run `just ci` rather than trusting this note.
70	
71	## 3. Root cause of the regressions, and the process fix
72	
73	The 8 bugs above were NOT random — every one of them is in the batch of pre-existing code found in
74	the working tree at session start (`e0cc091` "publish pipeline hardening", `60e0bef` "package-set
75	pattern resolution"), never Track F/G's own freshly-built logic. The audit independently confirms
76	this: Track F/G's code came through the sweep comparatively clean.
77	
78	**Why:** that batch was committed after checking only "does it compile, does clippy pass, do the
79	*existing* tests pass" — never run through canon→vector→lambda, never given a fresh adversarial
80	pass, never TDD'd. One of the bugs (`bca04b1`'s version-check) shipped with **zero test coverage at
81	all**, not even a happy-path test.
82	
83	**This is now a saved lesson** — read it before treating any future "found in the working tree"
84	code as done: `~/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/memory/feedback_found_code_needs_same_rigor.md`

88

96	Keep doing that explicitly in every reviewer prompt going forward.
97	
98	## 4. What's still open — the recommended next step
99	
100	Four test-coverage gaps the audit named explicitly, NOT yet touched by the remediation pass. These
101	are concrete, already-scoped, and cheap — either wire the code up with real tests or delete it if
102	it's genuinely dead:
103	
104	1. **`npm::round_trip`** (`crates/callisto-manifests/src/npm.rs:395-411`) — zero test coverage
105	   anywhere; its only reachable path (`preserve_npm_ranges = true`) is never set `true` in any test.
106	   Also rejects npm's idiomatic space-separated compound ranges (`>=1.0.0 <2.0.0`) with no test
107	   documenting this as intentional.
108	2. **`parse_publish_target`/`parse_release_trigger`** (`crates/callisto-graph/src/config/resolve.rs:148-163`)
109	   — only `"none"`/`"crates-io"` are ever parsed by any test; `"npm"`, `"pypi"`, `"nuget"`,
110	   `"github-release"`, and the invalid-string error path are untested despite being from this

112	   the exact current shape before writing tests.)
113	3. **`probe_git`/`check_git_version`** (`crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/git.rs:1-13`) — built to
114	   give a friendly `IncompatibleVersion` diagnostic for git < 2.20, but never called anywhere outside

116	   operation, or remove it if it's not wanted.
117	4. **`pre_cursor` tracking** (`crates/callisto-conventional/src/pre_cursor.rs:1-57`) — zero test
118	   coverage, and the field it would populate (`TagIndex.pre_cursor`) is hardcoded empty everywhere
119	   downstream. Looks like a half-wired, abandoned feature — wire it up with tests or remove the dead
120	   exports; don't leave it half-built.

11	Never treat "I found this code already written in the working tree, it compiles, and the tests that already existed for it pass" as equivalent to "this is verified." Only run canon→vector→lambda (or equivalent TDD rigor: red test written first, confirmed failing, then fix, then review) actually produces that guarantee — inheriting whatever coverage the original, unknown author happened to write does not.

It couldn't parse `version.workspace = true`, the exact pattern this repo's own 10 crates use, meaning `callisto publish` would fail on this repo today. `just ci` passed throughout because nothing ever exercised the function. A full adversarial audit (see [[project_workspace_audit_2026-08]]) later found 5+ more confirmed critical/high bugs concentrated in that same non-SDD-reviewed batch (`e0cc091`, `60e0bef`), while the code actually built this session via canon→vector→lambda (Track F, Track G) came through comparatively clean — direct evidence the pipeline works when it's actually invoked, and does nothing when it isn't.

At minimum: run a dedicated adversarial pass (proof:proof-scanner→proof-adversary, or bug-hunter) over it, and check whether its test fixtures actually exercise the shapes of data the target codebase itself produces (e.g. does a version-parsing test use `version.workspace = true` if the repo itself uses that pattern) rather than only synthetic happy-path literals. 10	
11	Do not distribute publish-pipeline fixes across parallel agents, even when they appear to touch different files.
12	
13	**Why:** Semantic coupling runs through shared traits (CommandRunner, RegistryClient), shared data flow (plan → load_plan → execute → publish), and activation dependencies (fixes that make previously-dead code live simultaneously). Parallel agents each see a slice and cannot reason about secondary effects in other agents' slices. A fix that looks correct in isolation can be a no-op or actively wrong given what another agent changed.
14	
15	**How to apply:** Fix the publish pipeline sequentially, one phase at a time, with full CI after each phase. Parallel agents are appropriate for *reading/investigation* (each agent reads a different slice, findings merge cleanly) but not for *writing* in semantically coupled systems.
16	
17	**Parallel investigation vs parallel fixing:** The 5-investigator audit workflow found 38 bugs effectively. That was parallel reading — correct use. The prior fix workflow (w08vr56yl) had one agent correctly fix Bug1 (publish order) while the order fix was a no-op because ManifestRole::Platform was never assigned — something a different agent was supposed to fix but in a way neither agent coordinated. Semantic coupling, not file overlap, is the constraint.

commit e0cc091821d8aea1aaad22848c8ab66e0dcf41f6
Author: Gabe Castro <gabe@techworx.dev>
Date:   Wed Aug 12 11:41:10 2026 +0200

    feat(publish): package filter, registry resolution, subprocess hardening
    
    Squashes several tightly cross-referential publish-pipeline changes that
    would not build standalone if split further:
    
    - plan_publish/publish gain a --package filter (errors on unknown names
      rather than emitting an empty plan) and convert previously-fatal git/
      changeset/tag lookup failures into soft Diagnostics.
    - npm publishConfig.access/registry is now read from package.json and
      respected over the scoped-package --access public default; fixes
      publishing to a private registry with publishConfig.access: "restricted".
    - SubprocessRegistryClient (publish_client.rs) now runs each publisher
      from the package's own directory instead of the workspace root, guards
      against publishing a version that doesn't match the plan, runs
      `python -m build` before `twine upload` (twine had no dist/ artifacts
      on a clean checkout), adds npm --registry / pnpm --no-git-checks / bun
      lockfile support, fixes PEP 427 wheel-filename normalization (dots
      weren't collapsed, only hyphens), fixes a false-positive rate-limit
      match on cargo's "429.1KiB compressed" summary line, and extends
      already-published detection to npm/twine E409 and mixed skip+upload
      output.
    - Publish orchestration caps rate-limit retries (MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES)
      so a 429 loop can no longer hang forever, adds a progress callback so
      `callisto publish` prints per-package status, and treats is_published()
      errors as non-fatal (falls through to attempt publish rather than
      aborting on a flaky pre-check).
    - CommandRunner gains run_with_timeout (default delegates to run(), so
      existing mock runners are unaffected); CliCommandRunner implements it
      with spawn+poll+kill and background-thread stderr streaming to avoid
      pipe deadlock. Used for the 300s publish subprocess timeout.
      New CommandError::TimedOut (E025).
    - PublishAttemptResult::Failed now carries a machine-readable `kind`
      (serialized as errorKind: rateLimited/authFailed/network/other) derived
      from RegistryError::kind_str(), so callers can distinguish failure

input.description: Read-only review of probe_git removal decision
input.prompt:
STRICTLY READ-ONLY REVIEW — you must not run `git stash`, `git checkout`, `git reset`, `git clean`, or any command that mutates the working tree or git state. Only read files and run non-mutating commands (cargo build/test/clippy are fine; git status/diff/log are fine).

Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (Rust workspace, `unsafe_code = "forbid"` everywhere).

Context: This is closing a named test-coverage gap: "`probe_git`/`check_git_version` (`crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/git.rs:1-13`) — built to give a friendly `IncompatibleVersion` diagnostic for git < 2.20, but never called anywhere outside its own definition and has no test. Wire it into `load_workspace` before any git-dependent operation, or remove it if it's not wanted." This is uncommitted in the working tree — do not commit it, just review it. Run `git diff` and `git status` yourself to see the actual change (it's a deletion: `git show --stat` won't work since it's uncommitted, use `git diff --stat` and `git diff`).

Unlike the other two gaps closed earlier this session (which added tests, and one of which fixed a real bug), THIS gap was resolved by **deleting** the dead function rather than wiring it in. What changed:
1. Deleted `crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/git.rs` entirely (was exactly 13 lines: just the `probe_git<R: CommandRunner>(runner: &R, cwd: &Path) -> Result<(), CommandError>` function, which shells `git --version` and calls `callisto_model::check_git_version` on the output).
2. Removed `pub mod git;` and `pub use git::probe_git;` from `crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/mod.rs`.
3. Left `callisto_model::check_git_version` (in `crates/callisto-model/src/exec.rs:94-122`) and its existing test (`parses_git_version`, exec.rs:128-133) completely untouched — that function already had test coverage and is not part of what was deleted.

**The reasoning behind choosing deletion over wiring** (please adversarially challenge this, not just confirm it):
- Grepped every `git` CLI invocation in `crates/callisto-vcs/src/shell.rs` and `access.rs` (the actual subprocess call sites for the shell-fallback git backend) and found no flag/feature that specifically requires git >= 2.20 — `rev-parse HEAD`, `tag --list`, `log --format=...`, `tag <name> <sha>` are all long-supported. So the `>=2.20` floor doesn't appear to gate any actually-used capability; it reads as an arbitrary "require something reasonably modern" floor picked at initial authorship, never connected to anything.
- There is no single existing call site that all git access flows through: `changed.rs`, `tags.rs` (via `TagIndex::build`), `aggregate.rs` (two places), `infer.rs`, `commands/tag.rs` in callisto-graph, plus `callisto-conventional/src/window.rs`, ALL independently call `callisto_vcs::GitAccess::discover(root, runner)` directly — there is no single funnel point in `callisto-graph` (e.g. `Workspace::load`) that all of these pass through, so wiring `probe_git` into `Workspace::load` would NOT actually guard most of these call sites, and would run even for commands that never touch git at all (violating the codebase's own documented lazy-cost philosophy, e.g. see the doc comment on `Workspace.tags: OnceCell<TagIndex>` in `crates/callisto-graph/src/lib.rs` explaining why `TagIndex` is built lazily rather than eagerly in `Workspace::load`).

result.output:
already-specified rules rather than adding a new one: §7.5's new-member exemption
(force-set to the group's current target version, no divergence error) applies exactly as
in normal mode, and at that same moment an `initialVersions` entry is synthesized for the
new member equal to the group's *current* `initialVersions` entry — giving it a proper
pre-release baseline retroactively rather than leaving it absent from `pre.json`. §7.5's
drift cross-check firing every run for the duration of the pre-release cycle until resolved
is expected behavior, consistent with how every other warn-by-default cross-check in this
spec works — no pre-mode-specific suppression.

**`ReleaseTrigger::Auto` packages in pre-mode** cannot be tracked via `pre.changesets`
(byte-compatible with `@changesets/cli`, which has no conventional-commits concept, so
`pre.json`'s schema has no field for "commits already counted" — and P1 forbids adding one).
This needs a marker distinct from §9.1's release tags — a release tag means "this got
published" (P2's stateless signal), which `version` never creates (§9.1, §13 invariant 24,
no exception). A pre-mode commit-boundary marker means something else entirely ("inference
already counted commits up to here"), so it's a **separate git ref namespace**, not a tag:
`refs/callisto/pre-cursor/<PackageId>` — written by `version` itself at the moment it
computes a pre-mode bump for an `Auto`-trigger package, alongside the manifest write (same
mutation phase, §7.6), and included in the calling workflow's existing `git push --tags`
step (§9.3) by pushing `refs/callisto/pre-cursor/*` alongside real tags — no new push step,
just a wider ref-spec on the one that already exists. Because it lives outside `refs/tags/`,
it can never collide with or be mistaken for a real release tag, so it doesn't need §9.1's
"only after success" rule at all — it's bookkeeping about *what inference already saw*, not
a signal about *what got published*. The next run's commit-based inference for that package
scans commits since this cursor ref, not since its last *stable* release tag — so
already-counted commits are naturally excluded without any new
`pre.json` field, and repeated `version` invocations in pre-mode are correctly idempotent
for `Auto`-trigger packages, the same way they already are for `Changeset`-trigger ones.

`callisto snapshot --tag <tag>` computes a transient, non-persistent version (e.g.
`0.0.0-snapshot-<sha>`) and writes it to manifests **uncommitted, untagged** — it never
creates a tag and never publishes (§9's coordinator posture applies here identically; an
earlier draft described `snapshot` as a "publish path," which was a leftover from the
pre-§9 orchestrator design and has been corrected). `snapshot`'s `--format json` output
carries the computed version and affected packages, not a `published`/`publishedPackages`
pair — actually publishing the snapshot manifests is the calling workflow's job, exactly
like every other publish in this design (§9.3's pattern). `snapshot` and pre-mode
(`pre.json` present with `mode: "pre"`) are mutually exclusive — invoking `snapshot` while
in pre-mode is a hard error, since both compute a version by a different, incompatible rule
from the same on-disk state.

# canon — Specification Skill

<overview>
canon turns requirements and research reports into unambiguous, testable specifications,
and turns defect class findings into architectural remediation specs. It enforces one
standard throughout: a developer who reads the output spec must be able to write an
implementation without asking a single clarifying question, and every acceptance
criterion must translate directly to a test case or type-level invariant check.
</overview>

---

<sub_skills>

### canon/draft
Given a `requirement@1` and optionally a `research-report@1`, produce a `spec@1` draft
with purpose, scope, non_goals, api_surface (if applicable), and acceptance criteria.
All criteria are testable propositions; error cases are covered with `is_error_case: true`.

### canon/verify
Given a draft `spec@1` plus the originating `requirement@1` and optional `research-report@1`, check whether each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts. Classifies criteria as supported, unsupported, or overfitted. Collects evidence only — does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Use this **before implementation** to confirm the spec is traceable to requirements.

### canon/drift
Given a spec@1 (via `spec_file_path`) and a workspace root, verify that the current code implements every acceptance criterion. Reads the spec from disk, reads the implementation from the workspace, and reports: `covered` (criterion is implemented and tested), `uncovered` (criterion has no matching implementation), and `drifted` (implementation exists but diverges from the criterion's contract). Use this **after implementation** to catch spec drift during maintenance — it is a diagnostic tool, not a blocking gate. lambda-exit-gate is the blocking gate; canon/drift is the ongoing health check.

### canon/audit
Given a `spec@1`, adversarially review it for untestable criteria, ambiguous language,
missing error cases, scope overlap, and incomplete sections. Returns a structured issue
list with specific rewritten suggested fixes.

### canon/gate
Given a `spec@1`, produce a binding pass/fail verdict before the spec enters planning. Default disposition is fail. On fail, returns specific blockers the drafter can act on without asking a follow-up question. On pass, the calling agent writes the spec to disk and sets `spec_file_path` — see the `<orchestration>` section.

### canon/architect
Given a `finding-report@1` from proof, produce a `spec@1` for the structural change that
eliminates the defect class — not a patch of individual instances but the abstraction
boundary, type invariant, or interface redesign that makes the class impossible to
reintroduce. This sub-skill closes the proof-to-design loop.

</sub_skills>

---

<artifact_contracts>

**Consumes**: `requirement@1`, `research-report@1` (optional), `finding-report@1` (canon/architect only), `spec_file_path` + workspace root (canon/drift only)

**Produces**: `spec@1` (written to `.claude/specs/<id>.json` by the skill orchestrator after gate pass; `spec_file_path` set to the workspace-relative path), `verdict@1` (canon/gate only)

</artifact_contracts>

---

<pipeline>

**Standard drafting pipeline:**
```
requirement@1 [+ research-report@1]
  → canon-drafter          (returns spec object — no disk write)
  → canon-verifier         (grounding check against source artifacts)
  → canon-auditor          (adversarial quality review)
  → canon-exit-gate        (binding pass/fail verdict)
  → [skill writes .claude/specs/<id>.json, sets spec_file_path]
  → spec@1
```

**On-demand drift pipeline (maintenance, any time after implementation):**
```
spec_file_path + workspace root
  → canon-drift-checker
  → drift report (covered / uncovered / drifted)
```

**Architectural remediation pipeline (invoked after proof):**
```
finding-report@1
  → canon-architect
  → canon-exit-gate
  → spec@1 (architectural)
  → vector → lambda
```

`canon-architect` is not part of the standard drafting pipeline. It is invoked when
proof returns a `finding-report@1` and the root cause requires a structural fix. The
output spec feeds back into vector for planning.

</pipeline>

---

<orchestration>

After `canon-exit-gate` returns a pass verdict, the calling agent MUST perform this step before handing off to vector:

1. Write the spec@1 JSON to `<workspace_root>/.claude/specs/<id>.json` using the file writing tool. Create the directory if it does not exist.
2. Set `spec_file_path` to the workspace-relative path (e.g. `.claude/specs/SPEC-001.json`) in the spec@1 object.
3. Pass the updated spec@1 — with `spec_file_path` set — to vector-planner.

This step is not optional. Without `spec_file_path` set, downstream agents fall back to reading the spec from conversation context, which is lossy under compression and cannot be independently verified.

</orchestration>

---

<framework_references>
- [Agent Best Practices](../../../shared/agent-best-practices.md)
- [Spec Schema](../../../shared/schemas/spec@1.json)
- [Verdict Schema](../../../shared/schemas/verdict@1.json)
- [Finding Report Schema](../../../shared/schemas/finding-report@1.json)
</framework_references>

---

<subagent_dispatch_matrix>

| Agent | Sub-skill | When to Delegate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`canon-drafter`** | draft | Producing a new spec from a requirement or research report. |
| **`canon-verifier`** | verify | Checking that each acceptance criterion is grounded in the source artifacts (pre-implementation only). |
| **`canon-drift-checker`** | drift | On-demand post-implementation drift check: reads spec from disk, reads code, classifies criteria as covered / uncovered / drifted. |
| **`canon-auditor`** | audit | Adversarial quality review for untestable language, ambiguity, and missing error cases. |
| **`canon-exit-gate`** | gate | Binding pass/fail judgment before handing the spec to planning. |
| **`canon-architect`** | architect | Designing the structural fix for a defect class surfaced by proof. |

</subagent_dispatch_matrix>

---
name: feedback-reviewer-must-actually-run-checks
description: lambda-reviewer and similar review agents sometimes self-report a check (e.g. "clippy clean") as passed without actually executing it; review prompts must explicitly demand real command execution and reading real output.
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When dispatching a `lambda:lambda-reviewer` (or any adversarial review agent) to check something mechanical like `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, do not trust a bare "clean, no warnings" claim in its report — during the SPEC-MANIFEST-PERSIST-001 track ([[project_manifest_persist_track]]), one reviewer (T15's review) reported clippy as clean when a real, live `needless_borrow` violation existed in the exact code it had just reviewed. The violation was only caught by the next task's reviewer, who was explicitly instructed to distrust the prior "clean" report and actually run the command.

**Why:** Agents can pattern-match "this is the kind of task where clippy is usually clean" and report success without invoking the tool, especially for tasks explicitly marked as having no production code change (which primes an expectation of "nothing to find here"). This is a silent-failure risk identical in shape to the kind of bug this codebase's own `bug-hunter`/`proof` agents hunt for in application code.

**How to apply:** When a review task involves a command-line check (clippy, tests, fmt, doc build), explicitly instruct the reviewer agent to "actually run `<command>` yourself and read the real output — do not just report clean based on inference." Once a false-clean report has happened in a track, call it out explicitly by name in every subsequent review prompt in that track ("a prior reviewer falsely reported X as clean — do not repeat that mistake") until the track ships. This pattern generalizes beyond clippy: any binary pass/fail claim from a review agent (tests pass, doc builds clean, no regressions) should be treated as unverified until the agent's own transcript shows the actual command output, not just its summary.

content.text:
That confirms the exact hazard. Key facts:

- `WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_version`/`write_dependency` still do combined mutate+persist in one call (never split like `Manifest` was in Spec A) — `cargo.rs:611-721`.
- The dual-targeting collision is real and reachable: a workspace root `Cargo.toml` that has one plain dependency and one `workspace = true` dependency produces, in the same `plan.rewrites`, both a `DepWriteTarget::Manifest("Cargo.toml")` entry (routed through the batchable `Manifest` trait) and a `DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency` entry targeting the same physical file (routed through `WorkspaceCargoResolver`'s separate, immediate read-modify-write). Today they're safe only because nothing is batched — each write is self-contained and sequential.
- `VersionWriteTarget::CargoWorkspacePackage` (the version-bump equivalent) has no production constructor anywhere — it's dead code today, so the version side of this collision is structurally unreachable. Only the dependency-rewrite side is live.

So the design question Spec B has to answer explicitly: what happens to a file that receives writes through *both* routing mechanisms in the same `apply_version_plan` call, once the `Manifest`-routed side starts batching (open once, mutate many, persist once)?

questions.question: How should Spec B handle a file that receives writes through both the Manifest trait AND WorkspaceCargoResolver in the same apply call (e.g. a workspace root Cargo.toml with one plain dependency and one workspace-inherited dependency both being rewritten)?

options.label: Exclude mixed-routing files from batching (Recommended)
options.description: Only batch (group+single-persist) files where every write for that path routes through the Manifest trait. Files that also receive a WorkspaceCargoResolver write in the same call keep today's safe, unbatched, immediate-write behavior for ALL their entries. Lowest risk — the collision this hazard depends on is narrow (root Cargo.toml only) and doesn't touch the common motivating case (N sibling packages rewriting one shared dependent's manifest, always non-root). Smaller performance win only in that narrow mixed case.

options.label: Order writes so the resolver always goes first
options.description: For any file targeted by both mechanisms, run all WorkspaceCargoResolver writes to it before opening the batched Manifest handle, so the handle's initial read reflects the resolver's already-flushed bytes. Requires restructuring apply_version_plan's write ordering to be path-aware across both loops rather than two independent loops. Delivers the full performance win everywhere but is a more invasive control-flow change with more surface area for a subtle bug.

options.label: Give WorkspaceCargoResolver the same mutate/persist split as Manifest
options.description: Extend the Spec A pattern to WorkspaceCargoResolver itself, then unify both routing mechanisms under one grouping-by-path mechanism with a single persist per file regardless of which mechanism did the mutation. Eliminates the hazard architecturally rather than by ordering, but is the largest-scope option — touches a type that was explicitly out of scope for Spec A, and is closest in shape to the original combined spec that triggered the first escalation.

Do not just patch wording superficially — verify each fix against the real current code yourself before writing it, the same way you did for the original draft.

## Blocking issue 1 (auditor): ManifestWriteGroup's stated algorithm silently drops the version-precondition check

Your api_surface entry for `ManifestWriteGroup` says the batched-write pass "applies handle.write_version(bump.1, permit) first (if bump is Some)" with no mention of the precondition check today's per-entry code performs BEFORE calling write_version (crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:82-91, still current): read `handle.current_version()`; if `current == bump.to`, skip write_version entirely (no mutation); if `current == bump.from`, call write_version; otherwise return `Err(GraphError::UnexpectedManifestVersion{...})` immediately. Verify this yourself by re-reading apply.rs:75-106 now.

A literal implementation of your current ManifestWriteGroup description would unconditionally call write_version whenever `bump` is `Some`, which would: (a) delete the safety check that the existing test `apply_returns_error_when_manifest_has_unexpected_version` depends on (a manifest at an unexpected version would get silently clobbered instead of erroring), and (b) spuriously persist (and increment persist_call_count) even in the already-at-target skip case, which today performs zero writes. Both directly contradict your own AC-009, which requires that test and `apply_is_idempotent_when_manifest_already_at_target_version` keep passing unmodified.

Fix: rewrite `ManifestWriteGroup`'s api_surface description to explicitly state the batched-write pass replicates today's three-way branch for the group's bump (if any) before touching any rewrite: skip (no mutation, proceed to rewrites) / write_version (mutate, proceed to rewrites) / return Err immediately (no rewrites applied, no persist called). Also add a new, distinct acceptance criterion — separate from AC-004, which only covers rewrite-failure — for "bump precondition fails inside a batched multi-entry group": assert the group's rewrites are never applied and persist is never called when the bump's current-version check fails.

## Blocking issue 2 (auditor + independently flagged by verifier): AC-012's "regardless of iteration order" claim is false

Your `api_surface.classify_manifest_writes` pins `ManifestWriteClassification.batched` as `BTreeMap<PathBuf, ManifestWriteGroup>` — iteration order is deterministic (lexicographic by PathBuf), not variable. Since `apply_version_plan` propagates errors via `?` (short-circuits immediately on the first Err), if the failing path P2 sorts BEFORE P1 in the BTreeMap, the function aborts on P2's failure before P1's group is ever attempted — so P1 would NOT be "reflecting its already-successfully-persisted batch" in that ordering; P1 would just be untouched original content, contradicting AC-012's own claim. The "regardless of order" claim is only true when P1 sorts before P2 (i.e. is processed and persisted first).

Fix: delete the "regardless of which path is processed first in iteration order" sentence from AC-012. Pin the fixture explicitly by choosing path names such that P1 sorts before P2 in the BTreeMap (guaranteeing P1 is processed and persisted before P2 fails), and state that ordering requirement explicitly in the criterion text itself so an implementer can't get it backwards.

## Medium issue 1 (auditor): AC-011's order-sensitivity proof has a weak-fixture loophole

The current "OR, at minimum, so that the final byte content is only correct under the specified sequencing..." clause is circular — it restates the requirement without forcing a genuinely self-verifying construction. A lazy implementer could use a fixture where the bump touches `[package].version` and the rewrite touches an unrelated `[dependencies].foo` entry (disjoint fields, byte-identical output regardless of order) and claim compliance by asserting "both changes are present" without ever proving order-sensitivity.

Fix: make the parenthetical example in AC-011 mandatory rather than illustrative — require the rewrite's DepSpec value to be derived from/equal to the bump's target version string (a self-referencing pin: e.g. rewriting a dependency's version requirement to match the package's own newly-bumped version), so that applying the rewrite before the bump would produce an assertably-wrong (stale-version) string. Remove the "OR, at minimum" escape clause entirely.

## Medium issue 2 (auditor): classify_manifest_writes's PathBuf-equality decision is under-justified against a real cross-module risk

You verified that for a given cascade.rs edge, `DepWriteTarget::Manifest(edge.from_manifest.clone())` and `DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency{root_manifest: edge.from_manifest.clone()}` share the same clone source (always match). But you never read or cited the SEPARATE code path that constructs `PlannedBump.writes`' `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest` paths — there's no evidence establishing that a given physical file's bump-write path and its rewrite-write path are always spelled identically (same join/normalize steps). If they ever diverge, mixed-routing detection silently fails — which is worse than not batching at all, since AC-005/AC-006 assume detection works, and this is the ONE mechanism protecting against the double-write hazard that caused the original spec's data-loss escalation.

Fix: find and read wherever `PlannedBump.writes`' `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest` paths are actually constructed (search crates/callisto-graph/src/ for where `PlannedBump` values get built — likely commands/version.rs, commands/snapshot.rs, or similar, based on the earlier investigation report's mention of "commands/version.rs:118-119 and commands/snapshot.rs:85 always emit VersionWriteTarget::Manifest(decl.path)"). Verify whether that `decl.path` and the rewrite-side `edge.from_manifest` are actually always the same PathBuf construction for the same package's canonical manifest. If you can verify they're always identically constructed, add that as a cited, falsifiable acceptance criterion (analogous to Spec A's AC-017 cascade.rs invariant test) rather than an unstated assumption. If you cannot fully verify it, add an explicit non_goals disclosure naming the residual risk plainly, OR specify a cheap, exact lexical normalization step (not full filesystem canonicalization) for the path comparison and state precisely what it does.

## Minor issue (auditor, optional but easy): non_goals wording gap

The "two or more distinct PlannedBump entries targeting the identical manifest path" non_goals item doesn't address a SINGLE PlannedBump's own `Vec<VersionWriteTarget>` containing two `VersionWriteTarget::Manifest` entries at the same path. Harmless (idempotent — both would carry identical (bump_index, target_version) data) but underspecified. Broaden the wording or add a one-sentence note.

AC-004 vs AC-012 are genuinely distinct scenarios per the auditor, not redundant — keep both. But it found 3 new blockers elsewhere that earlier rounds missed. Verdict: FAIL, retry_count 0 (first exit-gate submission) — please make one more revision to the SAME file.

## Blocker 1: AC-005's fixture is self-contradictory and cannot detect the bug it exists to catch

AC-005's fixture is "one plain, non-inherited dependency and one workspace-inherited dependency, both rewritten" — that produces exactly ONE Manifest-trait entry targeting P (the plain dep; the inherited one routes to DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency, not DepWriteTarget::Manifest). So "the count for P equals the number of Manifest-trait entries targeting P" evaluates to 1 — but the criterion's own point is to prove batching did NOT engage, i.e. it wants to show the count is "not 1" in the batching-would-give sense. With only one Manifest entry, open_call_count is 1 whether the exclusion guard works correctly OR is completely absent/broken — the test can't distinguish a correct implementation from a buggy one. This is the same "test that can't fail" defect class this whole session has been vigilant about (recall the T14-T20 red-phase-waived-task discipline in Spec A).

Fix: require the fixture to carry at least TWO plain, non-inherited dependency rewrites on P (two DepWriteTarget::Manifest entries) PLUS the one workspace-inherited rewrite (DepWriteTarget::CargoWorkspaceDependency{root_manifest: P}). Assert open_call_count() == 2 for P, with explicit text stating that a WRONGLY-batched implementation would incorrectly yield 1 (proving the assertion is discriminating). Update AC-006 to match — assert both plain deps' new specs plus the inherited dep's new spec in [workspace.dependencies].

## Blocker 2: AC-011 mandates a fixture that cannot be constructed — the ordering claim is provably false

AC-011 requires a fixture where applying the rewrite before the bump is "observably wrong" in the final bytes. The exit-gate read CargoToml::update_dependency_spec and CargoToml::write_version end to end: write_version writes [package].version; update_dependency_spec writes a dependencies-table entry using DepSpec::render() of a value that's a CONSTANT carried in SpecRewrite.to (precomputed in the plan, never read from the manifest at apply time). update_dependency_spec never reads the manifest's version. So the two mutations touch disjoint CST locations with plan-constant values — they are commutative. Even your "self-referencing pin" construction (rewriting a sibling dep to the bump's target_version) doesn't help, because the pinned string is already baked into the plan before apply_version_plan ever runs — it's not derived at apply time from whatever the bump did. No fixture can make bump-before-rewrites byte-observable, because it genuinely isn't, given how these two mutators work. Verify this yourself by re-reading both functions.

Fix: split AC-011 into two criteria. (a) Rewrite-internal ordering (genuinely byte-observable): mandate two SpecRewrite entries with the SAME RewriteKey (same target P, same dependency name, same kind) and DIFFERENT `to` values in plan.rewrites order; assert the final on-disk spec equals the SECOND one's value — this is only true if rewrite_indices is applied in plan.rewrites order, so it's a real, satisfiable test. (b) Bump-before-rewrites ordering is NOT byte-observable given the current mutators — don't try to prove it via output bytes. Instead ground it in the failure/skip paths that already prove sequencing exists: AC-014 (bump precondition failure means update_dependency_spec is never called — proves bump is checked first) and AC-016 (bump skip branch is evaluated before the rewrite step — proves the same). State explicitly that these two ACs together establish the sequencing guarantee, since no independent byte-level test is possible for the successful-bump-then-successful-rewrite case. If you want a stronger direct proof, consider requiring a call-order recorder/instrumentation in the test rather than an on-disk byte assertion — your call which approach is cleaner.

## Blocker 3: api_surface's ApplyOutcome.staged claim is factually false and leaves a real behavior decision undecided

Your apply_version_plan api_surface entry claims "ApplyOutcome.staged's contents and ordering semantics (one entry per distinct modified path, in the same relative order paths were first encountered) are unchanged." This is wrong on both counts, verified against the real current code:
1. TODAY: modified_paths.push(p.clone()) runs unconditionally per entry (apply.rs:97, apply.rs:122), and outcome.staged = modified_paths is assigned with NO dedup (apply.rs:335; the only contains() guard is for lockfiles at apply.rs:294). So today, N Manifest entries targeting the same path P put P into staged N times — "one entry per distinct modified path" describes neither today's actual behavior nor something this spec preserves.
2. AFTER BATCHING: your prescribed `batched: BTreeMap<PathBuf, ManifestWriteGroup>` iterates paths in lexicographic order, not plan-encounter order — so a plan with a bump on "z-crate/Cargo.toml" and a rewrite on "a-crate/Cargo.toml" would yield staged in a DIFFERENT order than today. ApplyOutcome.staged is a public field; no acceptance criterion currently covers it; every retained test uses .contains() so nothing would catch either change. An implementer has no answer to "does a batched path contribute 1 entry or N to staged, and in what order?"

Fix: correct the api_surface text to state TODAY's actual behavior (one push per entry, duplicates possible for a shared path, plan-encounter order). Then explicitly DECIDE the post-batching contract (the exit-gate's suggestion, which seems reasonable: one push per batched group — i.e. deduplicated for batched paths — labeled as a documented behavior change the same way AC-004 documents the all-or-nothing persist change). Add a new acceptance criterion pinning `staged` for the AC-001 multi-entry fixture (P appears exactly once in staged, not N times), and either pin the resulting ordering explicitly or state plainly that ordering is unspecified/not guaranteed for batched vs. mixed-routing paths.

## Non-blocking notes from the gate (use your judgment, not required but worth considering)

1. CargoToml::update_dependency_spec delegates to WorkspaceCargoResolver::write_dependency for a workspace-inherited dep, which loads+writes+persists the ROOT Cargo.toml as a side effect FROM INSIDE a batched group's rewrite step. The gate notes this is only safe because groups are opened/mutated/persisted strictly sequentially and Spec A's AC-017 guarantees no Manifest-routed rewrite is ever for an inherited dep. Consider stating "per-group open→persist sequencing is strictly sequential, one group fully completes before the next group begins" as an explicit requirement rather than leaving it implied by AC-012 — this matters because an implementation that hoisted all opens ahead of the group loop (a plausible "optimization") would reintroduce a stale-handle clobber, the exact bug class that killed the original combined spec.
2. AC-001/AC-002/AC-005 say "the counter... for path P" but the counters are process-global, not per-path — unambiguous given single-path fixtures today, but drop "for path P" for clarity since it could confuse an implementer.
3. Scope at 16 criteria across 2 crates/6 files is at the upper edge of one planning cycle but the gate called it coherent, not a fail reason — no action needed unless the eventual plan runs long, in which case AC-015's cross-crate test is separable.

Please verify all three fixes against the real code yourself (re-read the actual update_dependency_spec/write_version implementations for blocker 2, actual apply.rs:97/122/294/335 for blocker 3) before writing — same rigor as every prior round. Report back what changed.

You (or a peer instance) previously produced plan@1 for spec@1 SPEC-APPLY-BATCH-002, written to /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/plans/apply-batch-002-plan.json. Re-read the spec fresh from /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/specs/SPEC-APPLY-BATCH-002.json and the current crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs / crates/callisto-manifests/src/{lib,cargo,npm,python}.rs before making changes — verify each fix against real code yourself, don't just apply the suggested text mechanically.

## Issue 1 (task T09): DISHONEST red-phase waiver

T09 is in red_phase_waived_tasks but its own expected_failure text admits "This scenario WOULD have failed against the pre-Spec-B per-entry loops." Verified against apply.rs:75-130 (current, pre-T07 state): today's rewrites loop persists immediately after each update_dependency_spec call, and the bumps loop persists immediately after write_version. For T09's fixture (bump 1.0.0->1.1.0, rewrite helper->^1.1.0, rewrite nonexistent-dep->DependencyNotFound), the pre-T07 code leaves version="1.1.0" and helper="^1.1.0" on disk — so `assert_eq!(on_disk, original)` genuinely FAILS today. AC-004 is the spec's headline documented behavior change (all-or-nothing per file) and is one of only 3 is_error_case criteria in the spec (AC-004, AC-012, AC-014) — its red window is real and was forfeited purely by scheduling wrong.

Fix: remove T09 from red_phase_waived_tasks and re-sequence it as a new task (e.g. T06b) immediately BEFORE T07, so it has a genuine red phase against the pre-T07 code. Keep the test body. Set expected_failure to the real pre-T07 failure (the mutated file containing version="1.1.0" and helper="^1.1.0" instead of the original). Add AC-004 to T07's verify step so T07 is what turns this pre-written test green — note in T07's reasoning that it must make this pre-written test pass, not just its own new tests.

## Issue 2 (tasks T01/T02/T03): flaky counter assertions — process-global counter racing against 30 unrelated tests

T01/T02/T03 add tests calling reset_persist_call_count() then asserting persist_call_count() == 1, marked #[serial]. But #[serial] only serializes against OTHER #[serial] tests in the same binary — it does NOT exclude the ~30 existing non-#[serial] tests in `-p callisto-manifests --lib` that call `.persist(&permit())` (spread across cargo.rs, npm.rs, python.rs test modules, all in one process running in parallel threads). Any of those running concurrently between reset and read makes the assertion observe > 1. This repo already has the correct precedent documented: crates/callisto-graph/tests/apply_persist_open_count_test.rs's module doc says "Isolated in its own integration-test binary because callisto_manifests::open_call_count is a process-global counter that other, non-#[serial] tests in a shared binary would pollute."

Fix: move all three counter tests out of the `--lib` binary into a NEW dedicated integration binary crates/callisto-manifests/tests/persist_call_count_test.rs containing only those three #[serial] tests, constructing handles via the public `callisto_manifests::open(&decl, &ctx)` + `Manifest::persist` surface (all three types reachable that way). Update T01/T02/T03's test_command/verify_command accordingly (e.g. `cargo test -p callisto-manifests --test persist_call_count_test`). T01's red phase (E0433 on undeclared reset_persist_call_count) is unaffected by this move.

## Issue 3 (task T13): same flaky-counter defect, callisto-graph crate

T13's skipped-bump-plus-successful-rewrite test asserts persist_call_count() == 1 while placed in apply.rs's #[cfg(test)] module — that `--lib` binary has ~9+ other non-#[serial] tests calling apply_version_plan and persisting manifests in parallel. #[serial] doesn't exclude them. AC-016's spec text literally asks for the test to live "in apply.rs's #[cfg(test)] module" but that's exactly what this repo's own precedent (apply_persist_open_count_test.rs's doc comment) forbids for a process-global counter.

Fix: split the test. Keep the two byte assertions (version stays at target, helper becomes the new spec) in apply.rs's #[cfg(test)] module as a normal non-serial test. Move the `persist_call_count() == 1` assertion into a NEW #[serial] test in crates/callisto-graph/tests/apply_persist_open_count_test.rs alongside T07's/T10's tests. Add this file to T13's `files` list and record the deviation from AC-016's literal "in apply.rs" placement in T13's reasoning field so lambda-exit-gate doesn't flag it as a coverage gap later.
